newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends down in U.S., trade data sparks selling.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends down in U.S., trade data sparks selling.

text.p: *Dollar stood lower against most leading currencies at the close after news the U.S. trade gap widened a whopping 42.6 pct in July. Heavy mark/yen sells also in wake of trade data. *Rumors BOJ was in checking rates helped dollar pare some losses. *US housing starts due Thurs at 0830 EDT. Aug seen 1.445 million *Phil Fed Survey also due Thurs at 1000 EDT. Sept seen 21.0
The dollar ended lower after news that the U.S. international trade deficit unexpectedly ballooned by 42.6 percent in July, currency experts said.
The trade gap widened to $11.68 billion in July, the highest since the fourth quarter of 1987 when monthly deficits averaged $12.9 billion. June's shortfall was $8.19 billion.

"If you run a trade deficit, that basically means that you're importing more goods than you're exporting," said Bob Lynch, a senior currency analyst at MMS International. "It's going to create more demand for foreign currency than it does for your own currency. Hence the dollar becomes devalued."
The trade figures had surprised currency traders because Wall Street economists had forecast an overall deficit of $8.8 billion in July.
Dollar declines accelerated after the currency fell below key technical levels around 110 Japanese yen and 1.5120 German marks as previously set sell orders were triggered, currency experts said.
The dollar closed at 109.15/25 yen and 1.5090/00 marks, down from 110.11/14 yen and 1.5127/32 marks at the open.
The politically sensitive trade gap with Japan jumped 32.9 percent to $4.31 billion in July from the previous month.
Deterioration in this deficit prompted general demand for yen and traders also sold some European currencies and purchased yen.
"The real selling today has been marks for yen," said William Marr, manager of foreign exchange at Credit Commerciale de France.
The mark traded around 72.31/34 yen late in the day, down from about 72.81/84 yen in early dealings.
The bulk of the dollar's losses came shortly after the trade data were released.
Later in the New York session, rumors swept through the market that the Bank of Japan was checking the dollar-yen exchange rate with an eye to possibly buying dollars and selling yen, traders said.
"That in addition to an oversold condition short term caused the dollar to back up a little bit off the lows," said Debra Doerr-Larsen, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Commerzbank.
The Bank of Japan's New York office declined to comment on the market rumors.

France's conservative government presented on Wednesday a 1997 budget which aims to revive growth by cutting taxes while also reducing the budget deficit to guarantee the country a place in European monetary union slated to begin in January 1999.
"Government officials had pretty much leaked a good portion of that out to the press already," said MMS International's Lynch, adding the impact on the foreign exchange market was marginal.
Elsewhere, the dollar finished at 1.2415/25 Swiss francs, down from 1.2430/35 at the opening.
Sterling closed at $1.5602/09, up from $1.5588/95 at the start of trade.
The U.S. unit also finished at Canadian $1.3712/17, slightly weaker than C$1.3714/19 at the open.
The Australian dollar ended at $0.7881/86.
-- Donna Sells 212-859-1668
